Summary answer
Yes. From their first words, children do not just memorize isolated word–meaning pairs; they actively build and use semantic relations that connect words to each other and to experience. By infancy and toddlerhood, children detect taxonomic relatedness (e.g., “cat” and “dog” as similar kinds of animals), associative/functional links (e.g., “bone” and “dog”), and attribute/relational mappings (e.g., “apples” are “yummy” and “eatable”), and they leverage these relations to learn new words and refine existing ones in an expanding semantic network. <cite id="21053d42-0">A growing body of evidence indicates that even infants and toddlers are sensitive to semantic relations between words in their vocabularies, including both taxonomic and associative links</cite> <cite id="21053d42-1">Eighteen- to 24‑month‑olds show sensitivity to semantic relatedness (preferential looking/head‑turning), suggesting early processing of taxonomic relations and semantic organization</cite> <cite id="21053d42-2">Children use taxonomic structure to support novel word learning and build adult‑like hierarchical semantic networks from early vocabulary</cite> <cite id="5de30c91-0">Developmental studies support metaphor and conceptual mapping grounded in bodily/sensory experience, enabling children to form cross‑domain relations</cite> <cite id="5b466b22-0">Toddlers’ food‑related receptive lexicons predict acceptance of novel foods, indicating a growing lexical‑cognitive network for edibility and taste</cite> <cite id="5b466b22-1">Caregivers report rapid growth in children’s food words and non‑food eating words (e.g., “cup”), consistent with expanding relational schemas</cite>.

Do children learn relations among words?
Children rapidly detect when two heard words co‑occur with the same target (e.g., “cat” and “dog” pointing to similar animals) and when they are connected by functional routines (e.g., a “bone” used by a “dog”), indicating sensitivity to semantic relatedness beyond single-word meanings. <cite id="21053d42-0">Infants and toddlers show semantic priming/relatedness effects in intermodal preferential looking (e.g., faster orienting to a pictured target after “cat–dog” compared to “plate–dog”), with similar bilingual cross‑language effects; 24‑month‑olds show priming even for purely taxonomic pairs like “pig–dog” and for purely associative pairs like “bone–dog,” implying both kinds of relations contribute to structure‑building in the lexicon</cite>. <cite id="21053d42-1">At 18 months, infants already process taxonomic relations among words (i.e., their meanings and semantic organization), and 24‑month‑olds show semantic facilitation in relatedness tasks</cite>. <cite id="21053d42-2">Modeling and empirical work from 16–30 months support growth of the early lexical‑semantic network via lexical and semantic associations, indicating children use existing semantic structure to learn new words</cite>.

What kinds of semantic relations do they learn?
- Taxonomic/kind‑of relations. Children group words by natural kinds and subkinds (e.g., mammals like “cat” and “dog”). <cite id="21053d42-0">Semantic priming occurs for taxonomic pairs such as “pig–dog,” demonstrating sensitivity to “kind‑of” relatedness</cite>. <cite id="21053d42-1">By 18 months, infants process taxonomic relations among words, demonstrating early semantic organization</cite>.
- Associative/thematic (functional/situational) relations. Children exploit functional routines and scenes to connect words (e.g., “bone” used by “dog,” “plate” used with “eat,” “apples” associated with “yummy”). <cite id="21053d42-0">Associative/functional pairs like “bone–dog” yield semantic priming in monolingual and bilingual toddlers; even 24‑month‑olds show priming for purely associative links</cite>. <cite id="21053d42-2">Children incrementally encode connections between new words and existing entries, e.g., “hot” linked to synonyms (“sweltering”), antonyms (“cold”), and near‑synonyms (“warm/scalding”)</cite>.
- Attribute/relational mappings. Children learn predicates and properties that describe objects (e.g., “yummy,” “edible,” “eat-able,” “drinkable”) and connect them to objects like “apples,” “juice,” “spoons,” “cups,” “mouth,” “tongue.” <cite id="5b466b22-0">Larger food‑related receptive lexicons increase toddlers’ acceptance of novel foods, consistent with a growing lexical‑cognitive network linking sensory/edible properties to objects</cite>. <cite id="5b466b22-1">Expressive and receptive use of food words and non‑food eating words (e.g., “cup”) increases sharply from 18–24 months, reflecting expanding schemas for how objects relate to actions and properties</cite>. <cite id="5de30c91-0">Conceptual metaphor and blending accounts emphasize patterned mappings from sensory (taste) to abstract properties, with children learning by aligning concrete experiences (e.g., tasting) with words</cite>.
- Cross‑domain conceptual mappings and metaphor. Children relate seemingly dissimilar domains (e.g., “apples are blossoms” or “apples are sweet” as metaphorical mappings), which scaffolds later abstract relations. <cite id="5de30c91-2">Studies show children acquire primary mappings (embodied) and then generalize across concrete source words from the same domain, supporting across‑the‑board generalization once core mappings are in place</cite>.

How do children learn these relations?
Children leverage statistical structure in language and experience, aligning words with shared features, functional routines, and bodily states. <cite id="21053d42-2">As vocabulary grows, toddlers implicitly construct a web of connected words; they encode connections between new words and existing entries (e.g., “hot” linked to synonyms/antonyms/near‑synonyms)</cite>. <cite id="21053d42-1">Eye‑tracking and preferential looking reveal that infants use relatedness among heard words to guide attention to targets, indicating that word meanings are organized and retrievable via semantic relations</cite>. <cite id="5de30c91-0">Embodied accounts propose that metaphor and concept formation are rooted in sensory‑motor experience, enabling children to form patterned correspondences (e.g., from tactile/edible experience to words like “tasty,” “eat,” “mouth,” “tongue”)</cite>. <cite id="5b466b22-0">Naturalistically, exposure to foods and eating routines co‑develops food lexicons and broader cognitive schemas, with receptive food words predicting openness to novel foods</cite>. <cite id="21053d42-0">Cross‑linguistic and bilingual studies show semantic priming even when word pairs are taxonomically or associatively related, suggesting robust relational learning across languages</cite>.

Food-related examples: taste, edibility, and action verbs
Children learn that some objects are “yummy” and can be “eaten,” linking nouns, adjectives, verbs, and tools into a coherent schema. <cite id="5b466b22-0">Toddlers with larger food‑related receptive vocabularies accept novel foods more readily, implying that language about taste/texture/edibility integrates with real‑world eating experiences into a growing lexical‑cognitive network</cite>. <cite id="5b466b22-1">From 18 to 24 months, children rapidly expand expressive and receptive use of food words (e.g., “apple”) and non‑food eating words (e.g., “cup”), consistent with building relations among objects, actions, and properties</cite>. <cite id="21053d42-2">Incremental refinement of category boundaries (e.g., “cookie” coming to exclude cakes and crackers as contrasts emerge) mirrors how adjective–noun relations (e.g., “yummy cookie”) and verb–object relations (e.g., “eat apple”) are sharpened by contrastive language</cite>. <cite id="5de30c91-0">Conceptual blending accounts explain how children connect sensory experiences (taste, texture) to abstract relations (e.g., “sweetness” as a property of objects) and to metaphorical talk (e.g., “blossoming apples”)</cite>.

Do children learn “cat” and “dog” as similar, and “apples” as “yummy” and “eatable”?
Yes, with converging evidence. <cite id="21053d42-0">Infants and toddlers show semantic priming for related word pairs, including taxonomic pairs like “pig–dog,” demonstrating sensitivity to “kind‑of” similarity and associative links like “bone–dog,” and bilingual toddlers show cross‑language priming</cite>. <cite id="21053d42-1">By 18 months, infants already process taxonomic relations among words, indicating that they map related meanings and use semantic organization</cite>. <cite id="5b466b22-0">As children accumulate food‑related language, they become more open to novel foods, evidencing a learned network that includes attributes like “yummy,” actions like “eat,” and objects like “apples,” “spoons,” and “plates”</cite>. <cite id="21053d42-2">Children encode higher‑order relations (synonyms, antonyms, near‑synonyms) and refine categories through contrastive experience, showing that they learn not only single words but their relational roles in meaning</cite>.

Developmental trajectory and caveats
Sensitivity to word relations emerges early and becomes more sophisticated with vocabulary growth. <cite id="21053d42-0">Some studies argue early sensitivity to associative/functional links over purely semantic/taxonomic ones, while others find early taxonomic biases; both views agree that infants and toddlers exploit relational structure</cite>. <cite id="21053d42-1">By 18–24 months, children increasingly process taxonomic relatedness and show facilitation effects, with evidence of semantic organization</cite>. <cite id="21053d42-2">As vocabularies expand, reliance on taxonomic structure supports novel word learning, consistent with network growth</cite>. <cite id="5de30c91-2">Once primary mappings are in place, children generalize across concrete words within a domain (e.g., multiple source words used metaphorically), indicating abstracted relations become available for reuse</cite>. <cite id="5b466b22-0">Food learning exemplifies cross‑modal coupling of language and action: exposure to foods and eating routines shapes both acceptance and language</cite>. Two debates remain. First, whether early relations are primarily thematic (functional routines) or taxonomic (categorical kinds) varies by task and age, with evidence for both and for developmental change. <cite id="21053d42-0">Research reports an early advantage for associative/functional links, countered by studies emphasizing taxonomic preferences, but converges on early sensitivity to both</cite>. Second, the precise organization of early lexical‑semantic networks is still being refined; graph‑theoretic models and group comparisons suggest associative growth, but direct evidence before ~20 months is limited and mixed across paradigms and groups. <cite id="21053d42-1">Modeling suggests early growth via lexical and semantic associations; however, direct evidence of different lexical‑semantic organization before 20 months is lacking, motivating careful comparison across developmental groups</cite>.

Practical implications
Because children learn in a relational way, caregivers can scaffold learning by co‑occurring words and actions: naming objects (apple), describing attributes (yummy/sweet), and modeling actions (eat with a spoon), and by contrasting related and un‑related items (cat vs. plate; dog vs. cat) and contrasting predicates (yucky vs. yummy). <cite id="21053d42-0">Co‑occurrence of related words and pictures produces priming and faster orienting in toddlers, indicating that pairing supports relational learning</cite>. <cite id="5b466b22-0">Rich exposure to foods and eating routines supports acquisition of food‑related words and broader cognitive schemas</cite>. <cite id="21053d42-2">Contrastive language sharpens category boundaries and enriches semantic links (e.g., “cookie” vs. “cake,” “sweltering” vs. “cold”)</cite>.

Bottom line
Children do not merely memorize word lists; they learn a web of semantic relations—similarity (cat/dog), attribute–object mappings (apples are yummy/eatable), and functional routines (using cups to drink)—that guide comprehension, production, and rapid vocabulary growth. <cite id="21053d42-0">Evidence from infancy to toddlerhood shows robust sensitivity to taxonomic and associative/functional relatedness, including cross‑linguistic effects</cite> <cite id="21053d42-1">and early semantic organization detectable with eye‑tracking and preferential looking</cite> <cite id="21053d42-2">that supports network‑level growth and efficient word learning</cite> <cite id="5de30c91-0">consistent with embodied conceptual mappings and blending</cite> <cite id="5b466b22-0">and with food‑related language learning tightly coupled to real‑world eating experiences</cite>.

Title: For preschoolers, word knowledge falls on a continuum: A novel framework for capturing the incremental process of word learning.
Snippet: As children gain vocabulary knowledge, they implicitly construct a web of words that are connected to each other in meaningful ways (Collins & Loftus, 1975;Steyvers & Tenenbaum, 2005). Title: Tracking the associative boost in infancy.
Snippet: These investigations demonstrate children's sensitivity to both thematic and taxonomic relationships between pairs of objects, pictures, or words, though they tend to point to an early advantage for associative/functional/ episodic/thematic relationships over purely semantic/taxonomic ones, though it is worth keeping in mind that some studies have argued that children favor taxonomic relations over associative relations (Markman & Hutchinson, 1984;Xu & Tenenbaum, 2007). 

A growing body of evidence indicates that even infants and toddlers are sensitive to semantic relations between words in their vocabularies. In an intermodal preferential looking task, Arias-Trejo and Plunkett (2009) showed that 21-month-olds will look longer and orient faster to a target picture when it is preceded by a pair of semantically related words (e.g., cat-dog) than when preceded by a pair of semantically unrelated words (e.g., plate-dog). However, all these studies used related word pairs that were both taxonomically and associatively related. In a follow-up study, Arias-Trejo and Plunkett (2013) found semantic priming effects in 24-month-olds for word pairs that were purely taxonomically related (e.g., pig-dog) or purely associatively related (e.g., bone-dog), suggesting that taxonomic and associative links between words contribute to structure-building processes in the emerging lexicon.

Title: Stable organization of the early lexical-semantic network in 18- and 24-month-old preterm and full-term infants: an eye-tracker study
Snippet: A later study revealed the capacity of 18-month-olds to detect the semantic relatedness of acoustically presented words (Delle Luche et al., 2014). This head-turn preference study clearly demonstrated that at 18 months of age, infants already process the taxonomic relations of words (i.e., they process the meaning of the words and have semantic organization). A recent study revealed a semantic facilitation effect in 18-month-olds (Borovsky and Peters, 2019). Based on the early receptive vocabulary of infants and adult association norms, Hills et al. (2009b) modeled the graph-theoretic properties of the development of the early lexical-semantic network from 16 to 30 months of age. They contrasted different predictive network growth hypotheses based on adult data and concluded that early vocabulary growth is based on lexical and semantic associations (see also Hills et al., 2009a). We argue that there is no direct evidence for different lexical-semantic organization before 20 months of age, thus the contradiction might be resolved by the new paradigm and a systematic comparison of different developmental groups. 

To directly measure early knowledge representation differences, it is important to consider not only the vocabulary of the participants (their familiarity with the words) but also the type of semantic relation. Studies that have identified differences among 18-month-olds based on the size of their expressive vocabulary (Arias-Trejo and Plunkett, 2009;Rämä et al., 2013) used both associative and taxonomic relations. In 24-montholds and older toddlers, researchers have found sensitivity to thematic (associative) relations (Chow et al., 2017). Both taxonomies (classifications according to kind) and partonomies (classifications according to parts) are organizing principles for categories (Tversky, 1989). At the basic level, taxonomies can be constructed by means of the similarity of the members, making them easy for infants to acquire (Murphy, 2018). The acquisition of early perceptual categories by exposure to the members of two contrasting categories starts at 3 months of age (Quinn et al., 1993(Quinn et al., , 2001;;Quinn and Eimas, 1998).

Title: Lexical Leveraging in Novel Word Learning: Different Semantic Properties Support Learners at Different Stages of Development
Snippet: We explored the role that semantic category knowledge played in word learning while controlling for the availability of perceptual cues to meaning. From the prior work, it was unclear whether semantic density's impact on word learning could be attributed to higher-order conceptual organization or reflected lower-level perceptual overlap among category members. We found that, when controlling for the availability of perceptual cues to meaning, toddlers showed novel word learning advantages when they knew many other words in the semantic category to which the novel word belonged. Importantly, higher-and lower-density was defined in relation to each individual child's knowledge within the semantic categories we probed. This suggests that children build on higher-order conceptual structures to support word learning from early in development. In contrast to our a priori predictions, toddlers' reliance on taxonomic information did not increase with larger vocabularies. This demonstrates that 24month-old children, across a range of vocabulary skills, can use taxonomic structure to support word learning. More generally, these findings support the notion that taxonomic structure is available to children from early in life (see also Arias-Trejo and Plunkett 2013;Willits et al. 2013) and, thus, provides support for semantic network building that reflects adult-like conceptual hierarchies of knowledge.

Title: Metaphor Processing in Hearing and Speech/Language Sciences: A Narrative Review
Snippet: The embodied mind theory posits that the neural systems involved in sensory perception are essential for conceptual understanding. Metaphors are not confined to language; they encompass a significant portion of human cognitive activity. Title: The concept of ‘taste’in formation of Croatian and Turkish lexicon: A contrastive analysis
Snippet: Conceptual mapping of the concept of 'taste' onto abstract concepts can be subsumed under the more schematic conceptual metaphor MIND AS BODY, which Sweetser (1990) considers to be the overarching conceptual metaphor for all conceptual mappings between human sensory system and various mental and internal processes. 7 

The meaning 'to enjoy' is the least lexicalized meaning in IE languages. However, it is found in Sanskrit juṣáte, Latin gustare and French goûter, German kosten, and the opposite meaning 'disgust' is found in French dégoûter and English disgust. 8

Snippet: Acquiring abstract concepts-concepts that require extracting general patterns from more concrete or specific motor and perceptual experiences-lays the foundation for cognitive development across many domains. One example is the development of reasoning about relational categories-categories defined by roles or properties connecting multiple entities (Christie & Gentner, 2014;Gentner, 2016). Basic relations such as the concepts of "same" and "different" have long been considered "the very keel and backbone of our thinking" (James, 1890, p. 459), laying the foundation for abstract, combinatorial thought. Relational categories play a central role in reasoning across a wide variety of areas, including spatial cognition (Gentner et al., 2013;Loewenstein & Gentner, 2005) and mathematical reasoning (Singley & Bunge, 2014). Although recent evidence suggests that young children may have abilities to reason about relations such as same and different in certain contexts (Anderson et al., 2018;Walker & Gopnik, 2014), reasoning about relational categories remains quite difficult for children into their preschool years (Christie & Gentner, 2014;Hochmann et al., 2017). 

Past research has also investigated the development of children's ability to reason about categories that require learning a specific, usually abstract, category rule (Deng & Sloutsky, 2016;Kloos & Sloutsky, 2008;Minda & Miles, 2010). These studies often find limited or mixed evidence for rule-based category learning in children. On one hand, children between the ages of 3 and 8 can show adult-like category learning for rule-based categories when stimulus dimensions are transparent (e.g., successfully learning to group stimuli based on size as opposed to color; Minda et al., 2008). On the other hand, children around the same ages often fail to show robust learning when the stimulus dimensions are more opaque or difficult to identify (Rabi & Minda, 2014), when participants are required to learn category rules that combine information from multiple dimensions (Mathy et al., 2015;Minda et al., 2008), or when they are required to suppress a prepotent response or flexibly shift between category rules (Munakata et al., 2012;Zelazo & Carlson, 2012).

Title: Embodied language and early motor restriction: evidence from children with obstetric brachial plexus palsy and arthrogryposis
Snippet: Language deficits extended beyond action semantics. Children with OBPP and AMC showed reduced verbal fluency for animals, impaired object naming across multiple categories, and difficulties with object-object semantic associations (Koriakina et al., 2025). Here, three non-mutually-exclusive explanations deserve consideration. 

The first, grounded in the representational EEC approach, proposes that semantic categories in typically developing children are organized around multimodal clusters including perceptual properties, functional relationships, and action-based information (Unger et al., 2016). Consider the category of animals: while animals certainly possess distinctive visual features, they are also encoded through characteristic movement patterns (walk, run, fly, or swim) and through typical interaction affordances (pet, feed, or play) (Booth and Waxman, 2002). Similarly, object concepts are organized around the actions they afford: a hammer is represented not only through its visual appearance but also through grasping and striking actions (Gibson, 1979;Borghi, 2004). When motor experience is restricted from birth, this action-based organization may be weakened, compromising semantic network formation even for concepts with no obvious motor content. 

The second, based on the works by Iverson and colleagues on interactional EEC, proposes that children typically manipulate objects while caregivers provide labels and action descriptions, building multimodal associations among motor experience, perceptual features, and words (Iverson, 2010(Iverson, , 2021;;West and Iverson, 2017). Motor restrictions may disrupt these triadic interactions that normally ground semantic knowledge. Through thousands of such episodes, the child builds integrated semantic representations that bind together visual appearance, tactile properties, motor actions, object functions, and linguistic labels. Those episodes determine which objects become salient, generate rich haptic and proprioceptive information, and trigger the caregiver's linguistic input in a synchronized manner. Children with OBPP and especially AMC have fewer opportunities for independent object manipulation, thereby reducing these learning interactions from the very beginning. As a result, their semantic networks may develop with poorer and weaker representational connections, explaining why children with motor restrictions show not only specific action-semantic deficits but also broader impairments in semantic fluency, category fluency, and associative processing across multiple domains.

Snippet: Superordinate categories are based on abstract relations (Murphy, 2004). The properties that unite all the animals or all living things refer to the pattern of motion, and a combination of biological properties and processes that are abstract and not readily available perceptually. Most of the research on how structure mapping facilitates categorization refers to relational rather than entity categories. However, animal or living thing are entity categories. And yet, if any representations of entity categories are to be strengthened through comparisons, superordinates are the likely candidates. Graham, Namy, Gentner and Meagher (2010) showed how the comparison mechanism assists preschoolers in focusing on less obvious properties of objects when forming novel categories and that providing labels enhances the comparison effect. Gelman, Raman and Gentner (2009) asked children to list commonalities and differences for two objects that were either from the same ontological domain (two animals) or from different ontological domains (animal and an artifact). Children were prompted either by generic (dogs and cats) or specific language (this dog and this cat). The results showed that comparing objects from the same ontological domain prompted by generic wording made it most likely for children to generate deep rather than surface commonalities. Overall, the present findings fill an important gap in the extant literature.

Title: Eleven-Month-Olds Link Sound Properties With Animal Categories
Snippet: The goal of Experiment 1 was to examine 11-month-olds' ability to generalize the sound properties of cats and dogs to new category members, when familiarized with a single exemplar. We familiarized infants with two animal-sound pairings (one cat and one dog making their respective characteristic sounds) and then tested them in one of two conditions-the same breed condition and the different breed condition. Within each condition, infants were presented with two types of test trials. To evaluate the acquisition of the animal-sound mapping, same trials entailed the side-by-side presentation of the same two animals observed during familiarization, accompanied by one of the characteristic sounds (i.e., meowing or barking). Extension trials assessed infants' ability to extend the sound property to new category members and differed across conditions. In the same breed condition, infants saw new cat and dog exemplars that differed only in color from their counterparts during familiarization while one sound played. In this condition, we aimed to determine whether infants could make property generalizations to highly similar category members. In the different breed condition, infants were presented with new, less perceptually similar category members, reflecting a change in breed. By examining infants' generalization to less perceptually similar category members, we sought a more robust examination of infants' ability to establish category-property links, as opposed to solely shaped-based associations. This question is critical, given that despite sharing a number of key attributes [e.g., parts, shape, and texture; as identified by Rosch et al. (1976)], category members do not typically differ from one another solely in terms of color. We expected that, if infants formed an animalsound mapping and generalized the sound property to new category members, their proportion of looking to the target animal would be significantly greater than chance for both same and extension trials.

Title: Spatial Alignment Facilitates Visual Comparison in Children
Snippet: Other research has shown that infants also benefit from common labels in object categorization (Ferry, Hespos, & Waxman, 2010;Fulkerson & Waxman, 2007;Markman, 1989). Together, these findings suggest that common labels invite comparison, allowing children to gain insight into common structure. 

High overall similarity. Children (and adults) are more likely to spontaneously engage in comparison between similar items than between dissimilar ones. 1 Further, high overall similarity facilitates structural alignment (Gentner & Hoyos, 2017;Gentner, Loewenstein, & Hung, 2007;Gentner & Rattermann, 1991;Loewenstein & Gentner, 2001). Overall similarity matches (where object similarity supports the relational alignment) are easier to process than purely relational analogies for both children (Gentner & Toupin, 1986) and adults (Gentner & Kurtz, 2006). Overall similarity is particularly important early in learning, when children's representations are typically rich in objects but sparse in relations. Of course, close comparisons have the drawback that the common structure will typically be more concrete than with more distant comparisons. Distant comparisons (matching in relations but not object features) can support greater generalization-but only if the child can align them. However, studies show that carrying out overall similarity matches can highlight common relations, albeit in a rather concrete frame, and this can facilitate matching more distant pairs that share the same relational structure (progressive alignment) (Fyfe et al., 2014;Gentner, Loewenstein, & Hung, 2007;Gentner et al., 2011;Haryu et al., 2011;Kotovsky & Gentner, 1996;Thompson & Opfer, 2010). 

Spatiotemporal proximity. There is considerable evidence that children are more likely to compare and align two things if they are spatially and temporally juxtaposed. For example, in Christie and Gentner's (2010) study (described above), young children who compared two juxtaposed exemplars of a spatial pattern were able to abstract and transfer the pattern; but they failed to learn the pattern if the same two exemplars were shown sequentially.

documents.title: Eleven-Month-Olds Link Sound Properties With Animal Categories
documents.snippet: The goal of Experiment 1 was to examine 11-month-olds' ability to generalize the sound properties of cats and dogs to new category members, when familiarized with a single exemplar. We familiarized infants with two animal-sound pairings (one cat and one dog making their respective characteristic sounds) and then tested them in one of two conditions-the same breed condition and the different breed condition. Within each condition, infants were presented with two types of test trials. To evaluate the acquisition of the animal-sound mapping, same trials entailed the side-by-side presentation of the same two animals observed during familiarization, accompanied by one of the characteristic sounds (i.e., meowing or barking). Extension trials assessed infants' ability to extend the sound property to new category members and differed across conditions. In the same breed condition, infants saw new cat and dog exemplars that differed only in color from their counterparts during familiarization while one sound played. In this condition, we aimed to determine whether infants could make property generalizations to highly similar category members. In the different breed condition, infants were presented with new, less perceptually similar category members, reflecting a change in breed. By examining infants' generalization to less perceptually similar category members, we sought a more robust examination of infants' ability to establish category-property links, as opposed to solely shaped-based associations. This question is critical, given that despite sharing a number of key attributes [e.g., parts, shape, and texture; as identified by Rosch et al. (1976)], category members do not typically differ from one another solely in terms of color. We expected that, if infants formed an animalsound mapping and generalized the sound property to new category members, their proportion of looking to the target animal would be significantly greater than chance for both same and extension trials.

High overall similarity. Children (and adults) are more likely to spontaneously engage in comparison between similar items than between dissimilar ones. 1 Further, high overall similarity facilitates structural alignment (Gentner & Hoyos, 2017;Gentner, Loewenstein, & Hung, 2007;Gentner & Rattermann, 1991;Loewenstein & Gentner, 2001). Basic relations such as the concepts of "same" and "different" have long been considered "the very keel and backbone of our thinking" (James, 1890, p. 459), laying the foundation for abstract, combinatorial thought. Relational categories play a central role in reasoning across a wide variety of areas, including spatial cognition (Gentner et al., 2013;Loewenstein & Gentner, 2005) and mathematical reasoning (Singley & Bunge, 2014). First, in a study by James and Swain (2011), 5-and 6-year-old children were taught 10 novel verbs; half were learned while performing an action on a novel object, and half were learned through observation of the experimenter performing an action on a novel object. Title: Embodied language and early motor restriction: evidence from children with obstetric brachial plexus palsy and arthrogryposis
Snippet: Language deficits extended beyond action semantics. Children with OBPP and AMC showed reduced verbal fluency for animals, impaired object naming across multiple categories, and difficulties with object-object semantic associations (Koriakina et al., 2025). Here, three non-mutually-exclusive explanations deserve consideration. 

The first, grounded in the representational EEC approach, proposes that semantic categories in typically developing children are organized around multimodal clusters including perceptual properties, functional relationships, and action-based information (Unger et al., 2016). Consider the category of animals: while animals certainly possess distinctive visual features, they are also encoded through characteristic movement patterns (walk, run, fly, or swim) and through typical interaction affordances (pet, feed, or play) (Booth and Waxman, 2002). When motor experience is restricted from birth, this action-based organization may be weakened, compromising semantic network formation even for concepts with no obvious motor content. 

The second, based on the works by Iverson and colleagues on interactional EEC, proposes that children typically manipulate objects while caregivers provide labels and action descriptions, building multimodal associations among motor experience, perceptual features, and words (Iverson, 2010(Iverson, , 2021;;West and Iverson, 2017). Motor restrictions may disrupt these triadic interactions that normally ground semantic knowledge. Through thousands of such episodes, the child builds integrated semantic representations that bind together visual appearance, tactile properties, motor actions, object functions, and linguistic labels. Those episodes determine which objects become salient, generate rich haptic and proprioceptive information, and trigger the caregiver's linguistic input in a synchronized manner. Children with OBPP and especially AMC have fewer opportunities for independent object manipulation, thereby reducing these learning interactions from the very beginning. As a result, their semantic networks may develop with poorer and weaker representational connections, explaining why children with motor restrictions show not only specific action-semantic deficits but also broader impairments in semantic fluency, category fluency, and associative processing across multiple domains.

Objects and actions are fundamental semantic categories that are salient to infants already before they start learning their first words (Gogate & Hollich, 2016). Neural correlates of object and action word processing have been extensively studied but the extent to which word access and retrieval across the two categories is neurally similar remains under debate (for review, see Crepaldi et al., 2011Crepaldi et al., , 2013;;Vigliocco et al., 2011). 

Comparing object and action words (labelled grammatically as nouns and verbs) is not straightforward due to inherent differences between the two categories. Multiple semantic attributes (e.g., sensorimotor attributes, imageability, argument structure) as well as morphosyntactic attributes (e.g., thematic roles, inflection) separating them cannot be entirely controlled for: Behavioural differences in response times (RTs) in picture naming persist even after matching the stimuli, suggesting that verb representations remain more conceptually, lexically and morphologically complex (Kauschke & von Frankenberg, 2008;Szekely et al., 2005). This is further reflected in the neural signatures of object and action processing, with studies demonstrating that the differences between the categories become less pronounced when semantic-and morphological-level differences, in particular, are accounted for (e.g., Elli et al., 2019;Siri et al., 2008;Vigliocco et al., 2011). When the stimuli are well-matched, lesion-symptom mapping suggests overlap between object and action naming in the left temporal and parietal regions (Alyahya et al., 2018). 

On top of these intrinsic features, differences between the neural correlates of object and action word retrieval can be further exacerbated by experimental design (for more detailed discussion on the inherent and methodological differences between nouns and verbs see Crepaldi et al., 2011Crepaldi et al., , 2013;;Druks, 2002;Liljeström et al., 2008;Mätzig et al., 2009;Vigliocco et al., 2011). One such example is a classical visually guided word retrieval taskpicture naming.

judgment.criterion_reasoning: The answer fails to meet the verification criterion in a critical way. While it correctly states that the mechanisms are 'not identical' and documents different processes for taxonomic relations (cat-dog) versus thematic/usage relations (apple-eat), it does NOT explicitly reference the well-documented thematic-to-taxonomic shift in early childhood development. The criterion specifically requires mention of 'different developmental timelines' and 'the thematic-to-taxonomic shift.' The answer discusses developmental trajectories for each type separately (e.g., verb-patient mapping narrowing at 24 months, broadening at 36 months; comparative reasoning strengthening in preschool) but never frames this as a shift FROM thematic TO taxonomic processing. It treats them as parallel developing systems rather than describing the classic developmental pattern where young children initially prefer thematic associations (functional/script-based) before shifting to prefer taxonomic (category-based) associations around age 5-7. This is a foundational finding in developmental psychology that the answer completely omits.
other_issues: The answer conflates 'thematic relations' with 'verb-object usage associations.' While apple-eat is indeed a thematic relation, the question asks about thematic relations more broadly (which include script-based associations like dog-leash, cup-saucer) not just verb-argument structure. The answer focuses heavily on verb learning mechanisms rather than the broader concept of thematic vs. taxonomic relational processing.

None of the 12 cited papers directly address the thematic-to-taxonomic shift, which is surprising given this is one of the most well-established phenomena in semantic development (typically associated with researchers like Lin & Murphy, Smiley & Brown, etc.). The citations are tangentially related but don't provide the direct evidence the criterion demands.

The 'Convergences and divergences' section lists overlaps but doesn't clearly articulate that these are fundamentally different types of semantic relations (category membership vs. event/script-based associations) that are processed and accessed differently.
The answer is extremely long and detailed but paradoxically misses the central developmental phenomenon the question is asking about.
judgment.summary: The answer provides extensive detail about mechanisms underlying category learning (taxonomic) and verb-argument learning but critically fails to address the thematic-to-taxonomic shift—the well-documented developmental transition from preferring thematic to taxonomic relations. While it correctly states mechanisms differ, it doesn't frame this as the developmental dissociation the criterion requires. The answer also conflates thematic relations with verb learning rather than addressing script-based associations more broadly.
